newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian cabinet balance tilts towards reformers.
newsitem.headline: Russian cabinet balance tilts towards reformers.

text.p: The new cast of deputy premiers and the downgrading of some Soviet-style industrial ministries announced on Monday indicated liberal reformers have reinforced their position in the Russian government.
One conservative and one reformer among the four existing first deputies and nine deputy prime ministers kept their jobs in the new eight-man line-up of deputies and first deputies:
- Reformist Anatoly Chubais, one of two first deputy prime ministers in the new cabinet and appointed just 10 days ago, has also acquired the post of finance minister.
- Conservative Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Kulikov, keeps his post of interior minister.

Defining the relative political positions of Russian officials is problematic. But four generally conservative deputy premiers and three relatively reformist deputies lost these positions. Some will stay in junior posts:
These were the conservatives:
- First Deputy Prime Minister Alexei Bolshakov.
- Deputy Prime Minister Vladimir Babichev, demoted to minister but keeping the job of government administration chief.
- Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Zaveryukha.
- Deputy Prime Minister Oleg Lobov.
And the reformists:
- First Deputy Prime Minister Viktor Ilyushin.
- First Deputy Prime Minister Vladimir Potanin.
- Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Alexander Livshits.
Of four deputy prime ministers whose positions are harder to define, three -- Oleg Davydov, Vitaly Ignatenko and Vladimir Fortov -- lost their jobs and one -- Valery Serov -- kept it.
Fortov stays on as science and technology minister.
The new cast of deputy prime ministers is clearly dominated by reformists after five of them joined the cabinet:
- First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov, in charge of welfare, fighting monopolies and dealing with regional issues.
- Deputy Prime Minister Vladimir Bulgak, promoted from communications minister to take charge of technology and science.
- Deputy Prime Minister Yakov Urinson, promoted from deputy economy minister, who also becomes economy minister.
- Deputy Prime Minister Alfred Kokh, who also remains head of the State Property Committee -- effectively privatisation minister.
Somewhat less clear is the role of one new deputy:
- Deputy Prime Minister Oleg Sysuyev, mayor of the industrial centre of Samara.
No conservatives have yet been newly appointed.
Altogether the new cast of eight deputy and first deputy prime ministers has five reformers, one conservative and two technocrats whose positions are less clear.
Chernomyrdin said on Monday that some ministerial positions are still vacant and will be filled within the next week.
Interfax news agency quoted Kremlin sources as saying that the following important ministers would stay on:
- Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov.
- Defence Minister Igor Rodionov.
- Federal Security Service director Nikolai Kovalyov.

Another sign of pro-reform gains was the scrapping or downgrading of some Soviet-style economic management ministries, which Chubais and others had argued were hindering market reform or which were already obsolete after mass privatisations.
A Kremlin statement named the biggest of these as:
- The Industry Ministry is scrapped and its functions absorbed by the Economy Ministry.
- The Defence Industry Ministry is scrapped and its functions mostly absorbed by the Economy Ministry.
- The Construction Ministry is downgraded to a state committee for housing and construction policy.
- The Communications Ministry is downgraded to a state committee.
As a result of these actions, the three ministers, Yuri Bespalov, Zinovy Pak and Yefim Basin were all sacked.
The state committee on science and technology is upgraded to a full ministry.
Reformist Economy Minister Yevgeny Yasin who, unlike his promoted deputy Urinson, did not hold deputy premier rank, is sacked. The Kremlin said he would be given another post.
